Your Bankruptcy Fresh Start

Practical guide to life after bankruptcy discharge

Network › Your Bankruptcy Fresh Start

Most unsecured debts are discharged, including credit cards, medical bills, personal loans, and utility arrears. Debts that typically cannot be discharged include student loans (except in hardship cases), most taxes, child support, alimony, and debts from fraud or willful injury.

About This Site

Bankruptcy exists for one fundamental reason: to give honest but unfortunate debtors a fresh start. The Supreme Court has said so repeatedly, from Local Loan Co. v. Hunt (1934) to Grogan v. Garner (1991). But what does the fresh start actually look like in practice? What happens after you receive your discharge?

This site will provide a practical, honest guide to rebuilding after bankruptcy. We will cover credit rebuilding timelines (the discharge stays on your credit report for 7 to 10 years, but your score can recover much faster), how to handle creditors who try to collect discharged debts, and what financial habits protect your fresh start.

We will also address the emotional side of bankruptcy - the stigma, the relief, and the adjustment period. Too many bankruptcy resources focus only on the legal process and ignore the human experience. This site will cover both.

Part of the Open Bankruptcy Project - a growing collection of free, open-source bankruptcy information sites built on public court data. No advertising, no lead generation, no attorney referral fees. Real information, no strings.

## Buying a House After Bankruptcy [2026]: FHA 2-Year, Conventional 4-Year, and VA 2-Year Waiting Periods
Source: https://bankruptcyfreshstart.org/buy-a-house.html

Skip to main content

bankruptcyfreshstart.org

Home

First Year
Buy a House
Car Loan
Employment

Buying a House After Bankruptcy

Mortgage waiting periods by loan type - you will own a home again

Network › Fresh Start › Buy a House

FHA: 2 years after Chapter 7 discharge. VA: 2 years. Conventional: 4 years. During a Chapter 13 plan, FHA and VA allow applications after 1 year with trustee approval.

Mortgage Waiting Periods

Every major mortgage program has a specific waiting period after bankruptcy. The clock starts from the discharge date (for Chapter 7) or the dismissal date (if dismissed).

Loan TypeAfter Ch.7 DischargeAfter Ch.13Notes

FHA2 years1 year into plan (with trustee approval)Most accessible; 3.5% down

VA2 years1 year into plan0% down for eligible veterans

USDA3 years1 year into plan0% down; rural/suburban areas

Conventional4 years2 years after dischargeRequires stronger credit score

Jumbo7+ yearsVaries by lenderStrictest requirements

FHA Loans - The Most Common Path

FHA loans are by far the most popular choice for homebuyers after bankruptcy. Key requirements:

Waiting period: 2 years from Chapter 7 discharge date; or 1 year into an active Chapter 13 plan with court/trustee approval and demonstrated on-time plan payments

Credit score: Minimum 580 for 3.5% down payment; 500-579 requires 10% down

Clean credit since bankruptcy: No late payments, new collections, or derogatory marks

Stable employment: Typically 2 years of employment history

Extenuating circumstances exception: FHA may allow a shorter waiting period (as little as 1 year after Chapter 7) if you can document extenuating circumstances - a one-time event beyond your control (like a medical emergency or job loss due to employer closing) that caused the bankruptcy.

Preparing While You Wait

Open a secured credit card and build payment history

Save for a down payment (FHA requires only 3.5%)

Avoid any new derogatory credit marks

Maintain stable employment

Keep debt-to-income ratio low

Start Your Recovery

## Car Loan After Bankruptcy [2026]: Sub-Prime APR, Reaffirmation, and 11 USC 524(c) Rules
Source: https://bankruptcyfreshstart.org/car-loan.html

Skip to main content

bankruptcyfreshstart.org
☰

Home
Credit Rebuild
First Year
Buy a House
Car Loan
Employment

Getting a Car Loan After Bankruptcy

Auto financing options, interest rates, and how to get the best deal

Network › Fresh Start › Car Loan

Yes. Many lenders offer auto loans immediately after discharge. Interest rates start high (15-24% subprime) but improve as you rebuild credit.

Car Loans Are Available Immediately

Unlike mortgages, there is no mandatory waiting period for auto loans after bankruptcy. Many subprime lenders will approve car loans immediately after discharge. The trade-off is higher interest rates, but those rates improve over time as you rebuild credit.

Typical Interest Rates

TimingTypical APRNotes

Immediately after discharge15-24%Subprime lenders

6-12 months12-18%With on-time payments elsewhere

1-2 years8-14%Credit unions often best

2-4 years5-9%Approaching mainstream rates

Rates are approximate and depend on credit score, income, down payment, vehicle age, and lender.

How to Get the Best Deal

Save a down payment - Even $1,000-2,000 significantly improves your loan terms and shows the lender you are serious

Shop credit unions first - Credit unions often offer better rates than banks or dealership financing for borrowers with imperfect credit

Get pre-approved before visiting dealers - Know your rate before you negotiate so you have leverage

Focus on total cost, not monthly payment - Dealers can manipulate monthly payments by extending the loan term, which costs you more in total interest

Avoid add-ons - Extended warranties, gap insurance, and other dealer add-ons are often overpriced

Buy Here Pay Here - Proceed with Caution

Buy-here-pay-here (BHPH) dealers offer in-house financing with no credit check. The appeal is obvious for people with bankruptcy on their record. But BHPH dealers typically:

Charge 20-30% APR or higher

Sell vehicles at above-market prices

Require weekly or biweekly payments

Install GPS trackers and remote disabling devices

Repossess aggressively for missed payments

Better alternative: A secured credit card for 3-6 months plus a credit union pre-approval will almost always get you a better deal than a buy-here-pay-here lot.

## Bankruptcy Myths Debunked [2026]: 10 False Beliefs About Discharge, Credit, and 11 USC 525 Protections
Source: https://bankruptcyfreshstart.org/common-myths.html

Skip to main content

bankruptcyfreshstart.org
☰

Home
Credit Rebuild
First Year
Buy a House
Car Loan
Employment

Your Bankruptcy Fresh Start

Practical guide to life after bankruptcy discharge

Network › Your Bankruptcy Fresh Start

Exemptions are laws that protect certain property from being taken by the bankruptcy trustee or creditors. They cover your home, car, personal belongings, retirement accounts, and other assets up to specified dollar limits. Exemptions determine what you keep in bankruptcy.

You Will Never Get Credit Again

False. Credit card offers arrive within weeks of discharge. Auto loans available in 1-2 years. FHA mortgages after 2 years (Chapter 7) or 1 year (Chapter 13).

Everyone Will Know

Public record, but virtually nobody checks. Employers rarely search. Neighbors and friends will not find out unless you tell them.

You Will Lose Everything

Most Chapter 7 filers keep all property. Exemptions protect your home, vehicle, retirement accounts, household goods. Most consumer cases are "no-asset" cases.

You Can Only File Once

You can file multiple times with waiting periods between discharges. Check your eligibility at 1328f.com.

Check your eligibility

## COVID and Bankruptcy - Pandemic Debt Relief Options - Fresh Start
Source: https://bankruptcyfreshstart.org/covid-bankruptcy.html

bankruptcyfreshstart.org
☰

Home
Fresh Start
FAQ
Resources

COVID and Bankruptcy - Pandemic Debt Relief Options

Guide to bankruptcy options for pandemic-related debt. CARES Act protections, stimulus treatment, forbearance aftermath, and filing strategies for COVID debt.

Home › COVID and Bankruptcy - Pandemic Debt Relief Options

Bankruptcy Options for Pandemic Debt

If COVID caused job loss, business closure, or medical debt that you are still dealing with, bankruptcy may provide relief:

Stimulus payments: Federal stimulus payments received are NOT counted as income for the bankruptcy means test. They also do not need to be turned over to the trustee.

PPP and EIDL: PPP loans that were forgiven are not income for means test purposes. Unforgiven PPP and EIDL loans may be dischargeable if the business has closed.

Forbearance aftermath: If you entered mortgage or student loan forbearance during COVID, the deferred payments may have created a large arrears. Chapter 13 can cure mortgage arrears over 3-5 years.

Medical debt: COVID-related medical bills are fully dischargeable in bankruptcy.

## Rebuilding Credit After Bankruptcy - Fresh Start
Source: https://bankruptcyfreshstart.org/credit-rebuilding.html

Skip to main content

bankruptcyfreshstart.org

First Year
Buy a House
Car Loan

Rebuilding Credit After Bankruptcy

Your credit score can recover faster than you think

Network › Fresh Start › Credit Rebuild

Most people see meaningful improvement within 12-24 months with active rebuilding. Secured credit cards, on-time payments, and credit-builder loans accelerate recovery.

The Truth About Credit After Bankruptcy

The conventional wisdom is that bankruptcy destroys your credit for 7-10 years. The reality is more nuanced. For many people, their credit score actually increases within 6-12 months of discharge because the discharge eliminates the debt-to-income ratio problems that were dragging the score down.

A Chapter 7 bankruptcy stays on your credit report for 10 years. A Chapter 13 stays for 7 years. But the impact on your score diminishes significantly over time, especially if you actively rebuild.

Step-by-Step Credit Rebuilding

1. Get your credit reports

Within 30 days of discharge, pull your free credit reports from annualcreditreport.com. Check that all discharged debts show a $0 balance. Dispute any that still show a balance owed.

2. Open a secured credit card

A secured credit card requires a deposit (typically $200-500) that becomes your credit limit. Use it for small purchases and pay the balance in full every month. This builds a positive payment history. Many people qualify for secured cards immediately after discharge.

3. Consider a credit-builder loan

Credit unions and online lenders offer credit-builder loans where the money is held in a savings account while you make payments. When you finish paying, you get the money. The payments are reported to credit bureaus.

4. Become an authorized user

If a family member with good credit adds you as an authorized user on their credit card, their positive payment history may appear on your credit report. You do not need to actually use the card.

5. Pay everything on time

Payment history is the single most important factor in credit scoring (35% of FICO). Set up autopay for every bill. One missed payment can set your recovery back significantly.

Realistic Timeline

TimeframeExpected Score RangeTypical Milestones

At discharge500-550Score may actually increase from pre-filing low

6-12 months580-630Secured card + on-time payments showing

1-2 years620-680Eligible for unsecured credit cards, some auto loans

2-4 years660-720FHA mortgage eligible, better auto loan rates

4+ years700+Conventional mortgage eligible, competitive rates

Scores are approximate and vary based on individual circumstances, other credit factors, and scoring model used.

## Bankruptcy and Employment [2026]: 11 USC 525 Anti-Discrimination Protections for Government and Private Jobs
Source: https://bankruptcyfreshstart.org/employment.html

Skip to main content

bankruptcyfreshstart.org
☰

Home
Credit Rebuild
First Year
Buy a House
Car Loan
Employment

Bankruptcy and Employment

Your job is more protected than you think - Section 525 and beyond

Network › Fresh Start › Employment

Government employers cannot fire you solely for filing bankruptcy under Section 525(a). Private employers also cannot terminate you solely for bankruptcy under Section 525(b).

Section 525 - Anti-Discrimination Protection

Section 525 of the Bankruptcy Code prohibits certain forms of discrimination based on bankruptcy. It has two subsections with different protections:

Section 525(a) - Government employers

A governmental unit may not deny, revoke, suspend, or refuse to renew a license, permit, charter, franchise, or other similar grant; and may not deny employment to, terminate the employment of, or discriminate with respect to employment against a person solely because that person has filed bankruptcy or failed to pay a discharged debt.

Section 525(b) - Private employers

A private employer may not terminate the employment of, or discriminate with respect to employment against, an individual who is or has been a debtor under the Bankruptcy Code solely because of the bankruptcy. However, there is a critical gap: Section 525(b) does not explicitly prohibit private employers from refusing to hire based on bankruptcy.

The hiring gap: While government employers cannot refuse to hire you because of bankruptcy, the statute is silent on whether private employers can refuse to hire. Most courts have interpreted this silence to mean private employers CAN consider bankruptcy in hiring decisions. This is a significant limitation.

Background Checks

Bankruptcy is a public record. Employers who run background checks may discover it. However:

Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA), employers must get your written permission before pulling a credit report

If adverse action is taken based on the report, the employer must notify you and give you a copy

Some states and cities have banned or restricted credit checks in hiring (check your local laws)

Security Clearances

A common fear is that bankruptcy will cost you a security clearance. The reality:

Filing bankruptcy does NOT automatically disqualify you from holding a security clearance

Adjudicators consider the "whole person" - bankruptcy can actually be viewed positively as responsible debt management compared to ignoring debts

Unresolved debt is MORE of a security concern than bankruptcy, because it creates vulnerability to financial coercion

You must disclose the bankruptcy on your SF-86 form

Professional Licenses

Section 525(a) protects against government denial of professional licenses based on bankruptcy. This covers:

Medical licenses

Law licenses (bar admission)

CPA licenses

Teaching certificates

Real estate licenses

Commercial driver's licenses

A licensing board cannot deny or revoke your license solely because you filed bankruptcy. However, if the underlying conduct that led to bankruptcy also violated professional standards (fraud, misappropriation of client funds), the board can act on that conduct.

Know Your Rights

## First Year After Bankruptcy Discharge [2026]: Secured Cards, Credit Reports, and 7-10 Year Reporting Window
Source: https://bankruptcyfreshstart.org/first-year.html

Skip to main content

bankruptcyfreshstart.org
☰

Home
Credit Rebuild
First Year
Buy a House
Car Loan
Employment

The First Year After Discharge

What to expect, what to watch for, and how to protect your fresh start

Network › Fresh Start › First Year

Collection calls stop, garnishments end, and your credit score may actually improve as discharged debts show $0 balance. Focus on credit rebuilding and emergency savings.

What Changes Immediately

Collection calls stop - The discharge injunction under Section 524 permanently prohibits creditors from attempting to collect discharged debts. If they call, they are breaking the law.

Garnishments end - Wage garnishments for discharged debts must stop

Lawsuits dismissed - Pending collection lawsuits for discharged debts are typically dismissed

Debt-to-income improves - Your official debt load drops dramatically, which can actually improve your credit score

What to Watch For

Creditors who do not get the message

Some creditors continue to call or send statements after discharge. This is a violation of the discharge injunction. Keep a log of any contact attempts, including dates, phone numbers, and what was said. You may be able to recover damages.

Credit report errors

Check your credit reports 30-60 days after discharge. Discharged debts should show a $0 balance. If they still show a balance owed, dispute them with the credit bureaus in writing.

Reaffirmed debts

If you reaffirmed any debts during bankruptcy (typically car loans or mortgages), those debts survived the discharge. You are still obligated to pay them. Make sure payments are current.

Common Emotional Experiences

Bankruptcy carries a stigma, but the reality is that hundreds of thousands of people file every year. Common feelings in the first year include:

Relief - The weight of unmanageable debt is lifted

Guilt or shame - These are normal and they fade. Bankruptcy exists precisely because honest people face situations beyond their control.

Anxiety about the future - Will I be able to get credit? Buy a house? The answer is yes - it just takes time and deliberate effort.

Empowerment - Many people find that taking control of their financial situation through bankruptcy is empowering rather than defeating

Year One Action Plan

Pull credit reports and dispute errors (Month 1)

Open a secured credit card (Month 1-2)

Set up autopay for every bill (Month 1)

Build a 3-month emergency fund (Months 1-12)

Track your credit score monthly (use free services like Credit Karma)

Avoid new debt - live within your means

## Bankruptcy for Gig Workers - Uber, DoorDash, Freelancer Guide - Fresh Start
Source: https://bankruptcyfreshstart.org/gig-worker-bankruptcy.html

bankruptcyfreshstart.org
☰

Home
Fresh Start
FAQ
Resources

Bankruptcy for Gig Workers - Uber, DoorDash, Freelancer Guide

Guide to filing bankruptcy as a gig worker or freelancer. Means test issues, variable income, self-employment tax debt, and protecting your tools.

Home › Bankruptcy for Gig Workers - Uber, DoorDash, Freelancer Guide

Bankruptcy for Gig Workers and Freelancers

Filing bankruptcy as a gig worker presents unique challenges because your income is variable, you are self-employed, and your assets may include tools needed to earn a living.

Means test: The 6-month income lookback uses your actual gross receipts. Variable gig income can make timing your filing strategically important - file when income is lower.

Self-employment expenses: Legitimate business expenses (vehicle, phone, supplies) reduce your means test income. Document everything carefully.

1099 vs W-2: As a gig worker, you receive 1099s, not W-2s. This means no employer withholding, and you may owe self-employment taxes that have priority status in bankruptcy.

Tools of the trade: Most states have exemptions for tools, equipment, and vehicles used in your trade. These protect your ability to earn a living post-bankruptcy.

Chapter 7 vs Chapter 13 for Gig Workers

Chapter 7: Works well if your average income over 6 months is below the state median. Since gig income fluctuates, you can time your filing for a low-income period.

Chapter 13: Better if you have consistent gig income that exceeds the means test but need to restructure debts. The challenge is proposing a feasible plan with variable income - courts may require you to demonstrate income stability.

Tax debt warning: Many gig workers fall behind on estimated quarterly taxes. Self-employment tax debt may or may not be dischargeable depending on the 3-2-240 rules. Make sure you have filed all required tax returns before filing bankruptcy.

## Inheritance During Bankruptcy [2026]: The 11 USC 541(a)(5) 180-Day Look-Back Rule
Source: https://bankruptcyfreshstart.org/inheritance-during-bankruptcy.html

bankruptcyfreshstart.org
☰

Home
Fresh Start
FAQ
Resources

Inheritance During Bankruptcy - What Happens to Your Inheritance

What happens if you receive an inheritance during bankruptcy? The 180-day rule, estate property, exemptions, and how to protect inherited assets.

Home › Inheritance During Bankruptcy - What Happens to Your Inheritance

The 180-Day Rule

Under 11 U.S.C. Section 541(a)(5), if you receive an inheritance within 180 days of filing bankruptcy, it becomes property of the bankruptcy estate. This means:

The inheritance goes to the trustee unless you can exempt it

The 180-day window starts on your filing date and runs 180 days forward

The trigger is the date the person dies, not when you actually receive the money

Critical timing: If a family member is terminally ill and you are considering bankruptcy, the 180-day rule means that filing sooner rather than later may allow the inheritance to fall outside the window. Consult an attorney about timing.

Protecting an Inheritance

Exemptions: Some states have exemptions that can protect inherited property (wildcard exemptions, specific inheritance exemptions)

Chapter 13 timing: In Chapter 13, inherited property during the case becomes estate property under Section 1306, but you may be able to modify your plan to address it

Spendthrift trusts: If the inheritance is held in a properly drafted spendthrift trust, it may not become part of the bankruptcy estate

## Filing Bankruptcy Without Your Spouse [2026]: Joint Debts, Community Property, and Non-Filing Spouse Credit
Source: https://bankruptcyfreshstart.org/married-filing-bankruptcy-alone.html

bankruptcyfreshstart.org
☰

Home
Fresh Start
FAQ
Resources

Filing Bankruptcy Without Your Spouse - Individual vs Joint Filing

Can you file bankruptcy without your spouse? Pros, cons, and effects on joint debts, community property, and your spouse's credit when filing individually.

Home › Filing Bankruptcy Without Your Spouse - Individual vs Joint Filing

Filing Bankruptcy Without Your Spouse

You do not need your spouse's consent or participation to file bankruptcy. Many people file individually while married. Key considerations:

Separate debts: If the debt is in your name only, individual filing makes sense. Your discharge does not affect your spouse's credit or obligations.

Joint debts: Creditors can still pursue your spouse for joint debts after your filing. Chapter 13's co-debtor stay (Section 1301) provides temporary protection.

Means test: Your spouse's income is included in the means test even if they do not file. You can deduct their share of expenses.

Property: In common law states, only your property is included in the estate. Your spouse's separate property is not at risk.

Community property states: In AZ, CA, ID, LA, NV, NM, TX, WA, and WI, community property may be included in your estate even if your spouse does not file.

## Bankruptcy for Seniors - Guide for Retirees and Fixed Income - Fresh Start
Source: https://bankruptcyfreshstart.org/senior-citizen-bankruptcy.html

bankruptcyfreshstart.org
☰

Home
Fresh Start
FAQ
Resources

Bankruptcy for Seniors - Guide for Retirees and Fixed Income

Guide to bankruptcy for senior citizens. Social Security protection, retirement account exemptions, medical debt discharge, and special considerations for retirees.

Home › Bankruptcy for Seniors - Guide for Retirees and Fixed Income

Bankruptcy Protections for Seniors

Bankruptcy can be especially beneficial for seniors and retirees dealing with medical debt, credit card debt, or mortgage issues. Key protections include:

Social Security is fully exempt: Social Security benefits cannot be taken by the bankruptcy trustee or most creditors. This is protected under both federal and state law.

Retirement accounts are exempt: 401(k)s, IRAs (up to approximately $1.5 million), pensions, and other qualified retirement accounts are fully protected in bankruptcy under federal exemptions.

Medical debt discharge: Medical bills are the leading cause of bankruptcy among seniors. All medical debt is fully dischargeable.

Means test advantage: Many retirees have lower income (Social Security + pension), making them more likely to pass the Chapter 7 means test.

Special Considerations for Retirees

Home equity: Seniors often have significant home equity. Check your state's homestead exemption carefully. If equity exceeds the exemption, Chapter 13 (which always lets you keep the home) may be the better option.

Enhanced exemptions: Several states provide higher homestead exemptions for people over 65 or who are disabled.

Reverse mortgages: A reverse mortgage is not affected by a Chapter 7 filing. You keep the home and the reverse mortgage continues.

Judgment-proof analysis: If your only income is Social Security and you have no non-exempt assets, you may be effectively "judgment-proof" - meaning creditors cannot collect from you even without bankruptcy.

## Bankruptcy and Unemployment - Filing While Jobless - Fresh Start
Source: https://bankruptcyfreshstart.org/unemployment-and-bankruptcy.html

bankruptcyfreshstart.org
☰

Home
Fresh Start
FAQ
Resources

Bankruptcy and Unemployment - Filing While Jobless

Guide to filing bankruptcy while unemployed. Means test advantages, protecting unemployment benefits, and rebuilding after job loss and debt crisis.

Home › Bankruptcy and Unemployment - Filing While Jobless

Filing Bankruptcy While Unemployed

Unemployment can actually make bankruptcy easier in some ways:

Means test: Lower income makes you more likely to qualify for Chapter 7. The means test uses 6 months of income, so the longer you have been unemployed, the lower your average.

Unemployment benefits: Most states exempt unemployment compensation from creditors. Check your state's exemption laws.

Filing fee waiver: If your income is below 150% of the federal poverty guideline, you can request a fee waiver for Chapter 7 (Form 103B).

No garnishment risk: Without wages, creditors cannot garnish your income - but they can still levy bank accounts and file liens.

Strategic timing: If you just lost your job, your 6-month income average may still include months of employment. Waiting a few months until more unemployed months enter the lookback window can help you qualify for Chapter 7.

## Your Rights After Bankruptcy Discharge [2026]: 11 USC 524 Discharge Injunction and Anti-Discrimination
Source: https://bankruptcyfreshstart.org/your-rights.html

Skip to main content

bankruptcyfreshstart.org
☰

Home
Credit Rebuild
First Year
Buy a House
Car Loan
Employment

Your Bankruptcy Fresh Start

Practical guide to life after bankruptcy discharge

Network › Your Bankruptcy Fresh Start

Most unsecured debts are discharged, including credit cards, medical bills, personal loans, and utility arrears. Debts that typically cannot be discharged include student loans (except in hardship cases), most taxes, child support, alimony, and debts from fraud or willful injury.

Employment Protection - Section 525

Government employers cannot fire you or deny a license solely because of bankruptcy. Private employers cannot terminate you, though courts are split on hiring decisions.

Discharge Injunction - Section 524

Permanently bars creditors from collecting discharged debts. Phone calls, letters, lawsuits, garnishments, credit reporting - all prohibited. Violations can result in contempt and damages.

Government Benefits

Agencies cannot deny or revoke licenses, permits, or contracts solely because of bankruptcy. Federal student aid eligibility is not affected.

Learn about the discharge injunction

Discharge Injunction Guide

## Privacy Policy - bankruptcyfreshstart.org
Source: https://bankruptcyfreshstart.org/privacy.html

bankruptcyfreshstart.org

Home
Privacy

Privacy Policy

How we handle your data. Short version: we don't sell it, share it, or use it for advertising.

Data We Collect

We use Google Analytics (GA4) to measure aggregate site traffic. This includes page views, session duration, approximate geographic region (country and city level), and device type. We do not collect names, email addresses, or personally identifiable information through analytics.

Aggregate event data from Google Analytics is also exported to Google BigQuery for research use. The BigQuery data is used only for internal trajectory analysis and network health reports, is not shared with third parties, and is not used for advertising.

What We Don't Do

We do not sell data. We do not run advertising. We do not collect financial information. We do not use retargeting. We do not share any user data with attorneys, law firms, creditors, debt collectors, or legal service providers.

Specifically, we do not enable Google Signals, Google Ads integration, User-ID collection, or any cross-device tracking feature in Google Analytics. GA4 operates in aggregate-traffic-measurement mode only on this site.

Cookies

We use only first-party cookies set by Google Analytics for aggregate traffic measurement. We do not use advertising cookies, tracking pixels, or third-party analytics cookies.

Third-Party Services

Google Analytics (GA4) - aggregate traffic measurement

Google BigQuery - aggregate event data warehouse for research use only; not shared, not used for advertising

Google Search Console - search query measurement (clicks, impressions, our own page rankings)

GitHub Pages - hosting

Contact Forms & Email

This site may link to contact forms or email addresses operated by the Open Bankruptcy Project. Any data you submit through those channels is handled under the Open Bankruptcy Project master privacy policy, which governs all sites in this network.

Children's Privacy

This site is not directed at children under 13. We do not knowingly collect information from children.

Data Retention

Analytics data is retained for 14 months per Google's standard retention settings. After that window, individual event data is automatically deleted by Google; aggregate report metrics remain available.

Your Rights

You may request deletion of any personal data we hold by contacting info@openbankruptcyproject.org. California residents have additional rights under CCPA. EU residents have additional rights under GDPR. All such requests are handled by the Open Bankruptcy Project.

Network Policy

This site is part of the Open Bankruptcy Project operated by the Open Bankruptcy Project, a 501(c)(3) public charity (EIN 41-5159631). The same privacy standards apply across every site in the network. The authoritative master policy is maintained at https://openbankruptcyproject.org/privacy.html.

Changes

We may update this policy from time to time. Changes are reflected on the master policy first and then mirrored across all network sites. Check the master policy for the most current version.

Effective: March 30, 2026  |  Updated: April 11, 2026

Home  ·  Privacy  ·  Open Bankruptcy Project

Part of the Open Bankruptcy Project. Educational information only - not legal advice.

No ads. No affiliate links. No data sold. Supported by donations.

What This Site Is

bankruptcyfreshstart.org is an educational resource operated by the Open Bankruptcy Project, a 501(c)(3) public charity (EIN 41-5159631). It's part of the Open Bankruptcy Project - a collection of free, public-interest sites that translate federal bankruptcy court data, statutes, and procedures into language ordinary people can use.

The Open Bankruptcy Project

The Open Bankruptcy Project builds free, open-source tools that make public bankruptcy court data accessible to the people it affects most - debtors, advocates, researchers, journalists, and policymakers. Every screening tool, analysis script, and dataset is published on GitHub. Anyone can audit, reproduce, or build upon the work without permission or payment.

Our research is derived primarily from the Federal Judicial Center's Integrated Database covering all federal bankruptcy filings 2008 through 2024, cross-referenced with PACER docket data via the Free Law Project's RECAP archive and independent court-scraping tooling. Methodology and source code are public.

What This Site Is Not

This site is not a law firm. We do not represent clients, file bankruptcy cases, or give legal advice. We do not receive referral fees, affiliate commissions, or advertising revenue. We do not sell data.

If you need legal advice about your specific situation, consult a licensed bankruptcy attorney in your state.

Research Contributions

Our research supports two accepted suggestions to the Federal Judicial Conference Advisory Committee on Bankruptcy Rules:

Suggestion 26-BK-3 - procedural screening for 11 U.S.C. § 1328(f) re-filing eligibility

Suggestion 26-BK-5 - Rule 9037 / Form 121 / Form 309E1 amendments addressing systematic unredacted Social Security number exposure on federal bankruptcy dockets

Contact

General inquiries, data requests, research collaboration, and media: info@openbankruptcyproject.org

Privacy and Data Handling

See our privacy policy for details. Short version: aggregate analytics only; no data sold, no advertising, no attorney referrals, no financial information collected.

Home  ·  About  ·  Privacy  ·  Open Bankruptcy Project

Part of the Open Bankruptcy Project. Educational information only - not legal advice.

No ads. No affiliate links. No data sold. Supported by donations.

## Life After Bankruptcy in Alabama [2026]: Credit, Housing, and Fresh Start
Source: https://bankruptcyfreshstart.org/states/alabama.html

← bankruptcyfreshstart.org home

Life After Bankruptcy in Alabama [2026]: Credit, Housing, and Fresh Start

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Alabama residents.

Your Fresh Start in Alabama

The "fresh start" concept is the core purpose of consumer bankruptcy. Local Loan Co. v. Hunt, 292 U.S. 234 (1934), frames it as giving the honest but unfortunate debtor "a new opportunity in life and a clear field for future effort." In Alabama, the fresh start has three practical dimensions: debt extinguishment, asset retention, and credit rebuild.

The discharge order under 11 U.S.C. Section 727 (Chapter 7) or Section 1328 (Chapter 13) wipes most unsecured debts permanently. Creditors with discharged debts cannot pursue collection, sue, garnish, or even request payment under 11 U.S.C. Section 524 (the discharge injunction).

Alabama Federal Bankruptcy Data

Your fresh start begins when the discharge order enters. These Alabama numbers show how reliably Alabama debtors actually reach that order.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,743 consumer bankruptcy cases from Alabama's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 7478n/an/a

Chapter 131,265n/an/a

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Alabama Discharge Pattern

Federal data for Alabama is limited; the national baseline applies: roughly 75% of Chapter 7 cases and 45% of Chapter 13 cases reach discharge.

Post-Bankruptcy Credit Rebuild in Alabama

Credit rebuilding after a Alabama bankruptcy typically runs on this timeline:

Month 0-6: Secured credit card approved. Start with a $300-500 secured card, use it for $50-100/month, pay in full. Your FICO starts climbing.

Month 6-12: Second secured card OR a credit-builder loan. The two-tradeline rule pushes FICO above 620 for most filers.

Month 12-18: Auto loan available at subprime rates (12-18% APR). Shop carefully; avoid yo-yo financing.

Month 18-24: Unsecured cards become available. FICO typically 640-680 at this point.

Month 24-36: FHA mortgage eligibility (2-year post-BK wait for Chapter 7; 1 year for Chapter 13 in payment status).

Month 36-48: Conventional mortgage eligibility (4-year wait for Chapter 7).

Year 7: Chapter 13 falls off credit reports (FCRA 7-year rule from filing date).

Year 10: Chapter 7 falls off credit reports.

See detailed credit rebuilding guide.

Alabama Legal Aid and Re-Entry Support

Legal aid resources: Legal Services Alabama statewide; Jefferson County Volunteer Lawyers Program.

Housing consideration: Alabama has no statutory post-bankruptcy housing protection; landlords may consider BK in tenant screening unless local ordinance restricts.

Post-bankruptcy legal aid in Alabama typically covers: follow-up on discharge injunction violations, correction of credit reports, handling reaffirmation agreements, and defending against post-discharge collection attempts.

Buying a Home in Alabama After Bankruptcy

Mortgage waiting periods after Alabama bankruptcy:

Loan TypeChapter 7 WaitChapter 13 Wait

FHA2 years from discharge1 year in payment (with court approval)

VA2 years from discharge1 year in payment (with court approval)

USDA3 years from discharge1 year in payment (with court approval)

Conventional (Fannie Mae)4 years from discharge2 years from discharge / 4 years from dismissal

Conventional (Freddie Mac)4 years from dischargeSame as Fannie Mae

Non-QM / PortfolioAs little as 12 monthsAs little as 12 months

Alabama-specific factor: Alabama has no statutory post-bankruptcy housing protection; landlords may consider BK in tenant screening unless local ordinance restricts.

See full post-BK homebuying guide.

Alabama Employment After Bankruptcy

Federal law (11 U.S.C. Section 525) prohibits most employment discrimination based on bankruptcy:

Government employers (federal, state, local) are expressly barred from discriminating based solely on the bankruptcy filing.

Private employers cannot terminate an existing employee solely because of bankruptcy - but may consider BK in hiring decisions.

Security clearances and licenses generally continue post-BK; some require disclosure but rarely revocation.

Alabama does not add specific private-employer protections beyond Section 525. See post-BK employment guide.

Rebuilding Your Alabama Tax and Financial Profile

A Alabama fresh start also means cleaning up the tax and financial records:

Tax refunds going forward - post-petition refunds are yours; pre-petition refunds may be subject to the trustee's claim depending on timing.

1099-C exposure - bankruptcy-discharged debt is NOT 1099-C taxable income (Sec. 108(a)(1)(A)). This is a major advantage over settlement.

Schedule 1 reporting - federal forms include fields for bankruptcy-discharged amounts; use IRS Form 982.

Retirement contribution resumption - 401(k), IRA, and pension contributions were protected during bankruptcy; now increase them. Retirement is the foundation of permanent financial stability.

First-Year Mistakes to Avoid in Alabama

Common Alabama post-BK mistakes that undercut the fresh start:

Taking on high-interest debt too fast. Predatory subprime lenders target recent filers; payday and title loans are common traps.

Missing the reaffirmation window. Reaffirmation agreements on cars must be filed before discharge; missing this can forfeit the vehicle.

Ignoring post-discharge creditor contact. Collectors who attempt to collect discharged debt violate the Section 524 injunction; keep records and report.

Not reviewing credit reports. Discharged debts should show as "Discharged in Bankruptcy" with $0 balance; incorrect reporting is an FCRA violation.

Co-signing new debt. A co-signed loan that defaults puts your fresh start at risk immediately.

See common post-BK myths and first-year after BK.

Related Alabama Resources

First year after bankruptcy

Credit rebuilding steps

Buying a house

Getting a car loan

Employment after BK

Your post-BK rights

Alabama exemptions

Alabama means test

## Life After Bankruptcy in Alaska [2026]: Credit, Housing, and Fresh Start
Source: https://bankruptcyfreshstart.org/states/alaska.html

Life After Bankruptcy in Alaska [2026]: Credit, Housing, and Fresh Start

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Alaska residents.

Your Fresh Start in Alaska

The "fresh start" concept is the core purpose of consumer bankruptcy. Local Loan Co. v. Hunt, 292 U.S. 234 (1934), frames it as giving the honest but unfortunate debtor "a new opportunity in life and a clear field for future effort." In Alaska, the fresh start has three practical dimensions: debt extinguishment, asset retention, and credit rebuild.

The discharge order under 11 U.S.C. Section 727 (Chapter 7) or Section 1328 (Chapter 13) wipes most unsecured debts permanently. Creditors with discharged debts cannot pursue collection, sue, garnish, or even request payment under 11 U.S.C. Section 524 (the discharge injunction).

Alaska Discharge Pattern

Federal data for Alaska is limited; the national baseline applies: roughly 75% of Chapter 7 cases and 45% of Chapter 13 cases reach discharge.

Post-Bankruptcy Credit Rebuild in Alaska

Credit rebuilding after a Alaska bankruptcy typically runs on this timeline:

Month 0-6: Secured credit card approved. Start with a $300-500 secured card, use it for $50-100/month, pay in full. Your FICO starts climbing.

Month 6-12: Second secured card OR a credit-builder loan. The two-tradeline rule pushes FICO above 620 for most filers.

Month 12-18: Auto loan available at subprime rates (12-18% APR). Shop carefully; avoid yo-yo financing.

Month 18-24: Unsecured cards become available. FICO typically 640-680 at this point.

Month 24-36: FHA mortgage eligibility (2-year post-BK wait for Chapter 7; 1 year for Chapter 13 in payment status).

Month 36-48: Conventional mortgage eligibility (4-year wait for Chapter 7).

Year 7: Chapter 13 falls off credit reports (FCRA 7-year rule from filing date).

Year 10: Chapter 7 falls off credit reports.

See detailed credit rebuilding guide.

Alaska Legal Aid and Re-Entry Support

Legal aid resources: Alaska Legal Services Corporation in major hubs.

Housing consideration: Limited large-city housing market; rural tenancy often runs on oral agreements.

Post-bankruptcy legal aid in Alaska typically covers: follow-up on discharge injunction violations, correction of credit reports, handling reaffirmation agreements, and defending against post-discharge collection attempts.

Government employers (federal, state, local) are expressly barred from discriminating based solely on the bankruptcy filing.

Private employers cannot terminate an existing employee solely because of bankruptcy - but may consider BK in hiring decisions.

Security clearances and licenses generally continue post-BK; some require disclosure but rarely revocation.

Alaska does not add specific private-employer protections beyond Section 525. See post-BK employment guide.

Rebuilding Your Alaska Tax and Financial Profile

A Alaska fresh start also means cleaning up the tax and financial records:

Tax refunds going forward - post-petition refunds are yours; pre-petition refunds may be subject to the trustee's claim depending on timing.

1099-C exposure - bankruptcy-discharged debt is NOT 1099-C taxable income (Sec. 108(a)(1)(A)). This is a major advantage over settlement.

Schedule 1 reporting - federal forms include fields for bankruptcy-discharged amounts; use IRS Form 982.

Retirement contribution resumption - 401(k), IRA, and pension contributions were protected during bankruptcy; now increase them. Retirement is the foundation of permanent financial stability.

First-Year Mistakes to Avoid in Alaska

Common Alaska post-BK mistakes that undercut the fresh start:

Taking on high-interest debt too fast. Predatory subprime lenders target recent filers; payday and title loans are common traps.

Missing the reaffirmation window. Reaffirmation agreements on cars must be filed before discharge; missing this can forfeit the vehicle.

Ignoring post-discharge creditor contact. Collectors who attempt to collect discharged debt violate the Section 524 injunction; keep records and report.

## Life After Bankruptcy in Arizona [2026]: Credit, Housing, and Fresh Start
Source: https://bankruptcyfreshstart.org/states/arizona.html

← bankruptcyfreshstart.org home

Life After Bankruptcy in Arizona [2026]: Credit, Housing, and Fresh Start

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Arizona residents.

Your Fresh Start in Arizona

The "fresh start" concept is the core purpose of consumer bankruptcy. Local Loan Co. v. Hunt, 292 U.S. 234 (1934), frames it as giving the honest but unfortunate debtor "a new opportunity in life and a clear field for future effort." Arizona Discharge Pattern

Arizona Chapter 7 cases reach discharge at a strong 100.0% rate. Debtors who file complete schedules and attend their 341 meeting overwhelmingly receive a fresh start here.

Post-Bankruptcy Credit Rebuild in Arizona

Credit rebuilding after a Arizona bankruptcy typically runs on this timeline:

Month 0-6: Secured credit card approved. Start with a $300-500 secured card, use it for $50-100/month, pay in full. Your FICO starts climbing.

Month 36-48: Conventional mortgage eligibility (4-year wait for Chapter 7).

Year 7: Chapter 13 falls off credit reports (FCRA 7-year rule from filing date).

Year 10: Chapter 7 falls off credit reports.

See detailed credit rebuilding guide.

Housing consideration: AZ has no statutory ban on BK-based rental screening.

Life After Bankruptcy in Arkansas [2026]: Credit, Housing, and Fresh Start

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Arkansas residents.

Your Fresh Start in Arkansas

The "fresh start" concept is the core purpose of consumer bankruptcy. Local Loan Co. v. Hunt, 292 U.S. 234 (1934), frames it as giving the honest but unfortunate debtor "a new opportunity in life and a clear field for future effort." In Arkansas, the fresh start has three practical dimensions: debt extinguishment, asset retention, and credit rebuild.

The discharge order under 11 U.S.C. Section 727 (Chapter 7) or Section 1328 (Chapter 13) wipes most unsecured debts permanently. Creditors with discharged debts cannot pursue collection, sue, garnish, or even request payment under 11 U.S.C. Section 524 (the discharge injunction).

Arkansas Federal Bankruptcy Data

Your fresh start begins when the discharge order enters. These Arkansas numbers show how reliably Arkansas debtors actually reach that order.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 959 consumer bankruptcy cases from Arkansas's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 746296.7%3.3%

Chapter 1349760.9%39.1%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Arkansas Discharge Pattern

Arkansas Chapter 7 cases reach discharge at a strong 96.7% rate. Debtors who file complete schedules and attend their 341 meeting overwhelmingly receive a fresh start here.

Arkansas Chapter 13 discharges in 60.9% of resolved cases, above the national average. Plans are more likely to succeed here.

Post-Bankruptcy Credit Rebuild in Arkansas

Credit rebuilding after a Arkansas bankruptcy typically runs on this timeline:

Month 0-6: Secured credit card approved. Start with a $300-500 secured card, use it for $50-100/month, pay in full. Your FICO starts climbing.

Month 6-12: Second secured card OR a credit-builder loan. The two-tradeline rule pushes FICO above 620 for most filers.

Month 12-18: Auto loan available at subprime rates (12-18% APR). Shop carefully; avoid yo-yo financing.

Month 18-24: Unsecured cards become available. FICO typically 640-680 at this point.

Month 24-36: FHA mortgage eligibility (2-year post-BK wait for Chapter 7; 1 year for Chapter 13 in payment status).

Month 36-48: Conventional mortgage eligibility (4-year wait for Chapter 7).

Year 7: Chapter 13 falls off credit reports (FCRA 7-year rule from filing date).

Year 10: Chapter 7 falls off credit reports.

See detailed credit rebuilding guide.

Legal aid resources: Legal Aid of Arkansas; Center for Arkansas Legal Services.

Housing consideration: No specific state protection against BK-based tenant screening.

Source: https://bankruptcyfreshstart.org/states/california.html

← bankruptcyfreshstart.org home

Life After Bankruptcy in California [2026]: Credit, Housing, and Fresh Start

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for California residents.

Your Fresh Start in California

The "fresh start" concept is the core purpose of consumer bankruptcy. Local Loan Co. v. Hunt, 292 U.S. 234 (1934), frames it as giving the honest but unfortunate debtor "a new opportunity in life and a clear field for future effort." In California, the fresh start has three practical dimensions: debt extinguishment, asset retention, and credit rebuild.

The discharge order under 11 U.S.C. Section 727 (Chapter 7) or Section 1328 (Chapter 13) wipes most unsecured debts permanently. Creditors with discharged debts cannot pursue collection, sue, garnish, or even request payment under 11 U.S.C. Section 524 (the discharge injunction).

California Federal Bankruptcy Data

Your fresh start begins when the discharge order enters. These California numbers show how reliably California debtors actually reach that order.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 6,723 consumer bankruptcy cases from California's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 75,80898.4%1.6%

Chapter 1391538.8%61.2%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

California Discharge Pattern

California Chapter 7 cases reach discharge at a strong 98.4% rate. Debtors who file complete schedules and attend their 341 meeting overwhelmingly receive a fresh start here.

California Chapter 13 discharge rate of 38.8% is typical. Realistic budget assumptions are the main factor in plan survival.

Post-Bankruptcy Credit Rebuild in California

Credit rebuilding after a California bankruptcy typically runs on this timeline:

Month 0-6: Secured credit card approved. Start with a $300-500 secured card, use it for $50-100/month, pay in full. Your FICO starts climbing.

Month 6-12: Second secured card OR a credit-builder loan. The two-tradeline rule pushes FICO above 620 for most filers.

Month 12-18: Auto loan available at subprime rates (12-18% APR). Shop carefully; avoid yo-yo financing.

Month 18-24: Unsecured cards become available. FICO typically 640-680 at this point.

Month 24-36: FHA mortgage eligibility (2-year post-BK wait for Chapter 7; 1 year for Chapter 13 in payment status).

Month 36-48: Conventional mortgage eligibility (4-year wait for Chapter 7).

Year 7: Chapter 13 falls off credit reports (FCRA 7-year rule from filing date).

Year 10: Chapter 7 falls off credit reports.

See detailed credit rebuilding guide.

California Legal Aid and Re-Entry Support

Legal aid resources: California Legal Services in multiple regions; Legal Aid at Work; BayLegal.

Housing consideration: CA Civil Code Section 1785.13 restricts BK reporting to 7 years (shorter than federal FCRA).

Post-bankruptcy legal aid in California typically covers: follow-up on discharge injunction violations, correction of credit reports, handling reaffirmation agreements, and defending against post-discharge collection attempts.

Government employers (federal, state, local) are expressly barred from discriminating based solely on the bankruptcy filing.

Private employers cannot terminate an existing employee solely because of bankruptcy - but may consider BK in hiring decisions.

Tax refunds going forward - post-petition refunds are yours; pre-petition refunds may be subject to the trustee's claim depending on timing.

Taking on high-interest debt too fast. Predatory subprime lenders target recent filers; payday and title loans are common traps.

Missing the reaffirmation window. Reaffirmation agreements on cars must be filed before discharge; missing this can forfeit the vehicle.

Ignoring post-discharge creditor contact. Collectors who attempt to collect discharged debt violate the Section 524 injunction; keep records and report.

Not reviewing credit reports. Discharged debts should show as "Discharged in Bankruptcy" with $0 balance; incorrect reporting is an FCRA violation.

Co-signing new debt. A co-signed loan that defaults puts your fresh start at risk immediately.

See common post-BK myths and first-year after BK.

## Life After Bankruptcy in Colorado [2026]: Credit, Housing, and Fresh Start
Source: https://bankruptcyfreshstart.org/states/colorado.html

← bankruptcyfreshstart.org home

Life After Bankruptcy in Colorado [2026]: Credit, Housing, and Fresh Start

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Colorado residents.

Your Fresh Start in Colorado

The "fresh start" concept is the core purpose of consumer bankruptcy. Local Loan Co. v. Hunt, 292 U.S. 234 (1934), frames it as giving the honest but unfortunate debtor "a new opportunity in life and a clear field for future effort." In Colorado, the fresh start has three practical dimensions: debt extinguishment, asset retention, and credit rebuild.

The discharge order under 11 U.S.C. Section 727 (Chapter 7) or Section 1328 (Chapter 13) wipes most unsecured debts permanently. Creditors with discharged debts cannot pursue collection, sue, garnish, or even request payment under 11 U.S.C. Section 524 (the discharge injunction).

Colorado Federal Bankruptcy Data

Your fresh start begins when the discharge order enters. These Colorado numbers show how reliably Colorado debtors actually reach that order.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 86 consumer bankruptcy cases from Colorado's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 78498.8%1.2%

Chapter 132n/an/a

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Colorado Discharge Pattern

Colorado Chapter 7 cases reach discharge at a strong 98.8% rate. Debtors who file complete schedules and attend their 341 meeting overwhelmingly receive a fresh start here.

Post-Bankruptcy Credit Rebuild in Colorado

Credit rebuilding after a Colorado bankruptcy typically runs on this timeline:

Month 0-6: Secured credit card approved. Start with a $300-500 secured card, use it for $50-100/month, pay in full. Your FICO starts climbing.

Month 6-12: Second secured card OR a credit-builder loan. The two-tradeline rule pushes FICO above 620 for most filers.

Month 12-18: Auto loan available at subprime rates (12-18% APR). Shop carefully; avoid yo-yo financing.

Month 18-24: Unsecured cards become available. FICO typically 640-680 at this point.

Month 24-36: FHA mortgage eligibility (2-year post-BK wait for Chapter 7; 1 year for Chapter 13 in payment status).

Month 36-48: Conventional mortgage eligibility (4-year wait for Chapter 7).

Year 7: Chapter 13 falls off credit reports (FCRA 7-year rule from filing date).

Year 10: Chapter 7 falls off credit reports.

See detailed credit rebuilding guide.

Colorado Legal Aid and Re-Entry Support

Legal aid resources: Colorado Legal Services statewide.

Housing consideration: No state-specific BK-tenant protection; strong general tenant protections apply.

Post-bankruptcy legal aid in Colorado typically covers: follow-up on discharge injunction violations, correction of credit reports, handling reaffirmation agreements, and defending against post-discharge collection attempts.

Buying a Home in Colorado After Bankruptcy

Mortgage waiting periods after Colorado bankruptcy:

Loan TypeChapter 7 WaitChapter 13 Wait

FHA2 years from discharge1 year in payment (with court approval)

VA2 years from discharge1 year in payment (with court approval)

USDA3 years from discharge1 year in payment (with court approval)

Conventional (Fannie Mae)4 years from discharge2 years from discharge / 4 years from dismissal

Conventional (Freddie Mac)4 years from dischargeSame as Fannie Mae

Non-QM / PortfolioAs little as 12 monthsAs little as 12 months

Colorado-specific factor: No state-specific BK-tenant protection; strong general tenant protections apply.

See full post-BK homebuying guide.

Colorado Employment After Bankruptcy

Federal law (11 U.S.C. Section 525) prohibits most employment discrimination based on bankruptcy:

Government employers (federal, state, local) are expressly barred from discriminating based solely on the bankruptcy filing.

Private employers cannot terminate an existing employee solely because of bankruptcy - but may consider BK in hiring decisions.

Security clearances and licenses generally continue post-BK; some require disclosure but rarely revocation.

Colorado does not add specific private-employer protections beyond Section 525. See post-BK employment guide.

Rebuilding Your Colorado Tax and Financial Profile

A Colorado fresh start also means cleaning up the tax and financial records:

Tax refunds going forward - post-petition refunds are yours; pre-petition refunds may be subject to the trustee's claim depending on timing.

1099-C exposure - bankruptcy-discharged debt is NOT 1099-C taxable income (Sec. 108(a)(1)(A)). This is a major advantage over settlement.

Schedule 1 reporting - federal forms include fields for bankruptcy-discharged amounts; use IRS Form 982.

Retirement contribution resumption - 401(k), IRA, and pension contributions were protected during bankruptcy; now increase them. Retirement is the foundation of permanent financial stability.

First-Year Mistakes to Avoid in Colorado

Common Colorado post-BK mistakes that undercut the fresh start:

Taking on high-interest debt too fast. Predatory subprime lenders target recent filers; payday and title loans are common traps.

Missing the reaffirmation window. Reaffirmation agreements on cars must be filed before discharge; missing this can forfeit the vehicle.

Ignoring post-discharge creditor contact. Collectors who attempt to collect discharged debt violate the Section 524 injunction; keep records and report.

Not reviewing credit reports. Discharged debts should show as "Discharged in Bankruptcy" with $0 balance; incorrect reporting is an FCRA violation.

Co-signing new debt. A co-signed loan that defaults puts your fresh start at risk immediately.

See common post-BK myths and first-year after BK.

Related Colorado Resources

Your post-BK rights

Colorado exemptions

Colorado means test

## Life After Bankruptcy in Georgia [2026]: Credit, Housing, and Fresh Start
Source: https://bankruptcyfreshstart.org/states/georgia.html

← bankruptcyfreshstart.org home

Life After Bankruptcy in Georgia [2026]: Credit, Housing, and Fresh Start

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Georgia residents.

Your Fresh Start in Georgia

The "fresh start" concept is the core purpose of consumer bankruptcy. Local Loan Co. v. Hunt, 292 U.S. 234 (1934), frames it as giving the honest but unfortunate debtor "a new opportunity in life and a clear field for future effort." In Georgia, the fresh start has three practical dimensions: debt extinguishment, asset retention, and credit rebuild.

The discharge order under 11 U.S.C. Section 727 (Chapter 7) or Section 1328 (Chapter 13) wipes most unsecured debts permanently. Creditors with discharged debts cannot pursue collection, sue, garnish, or even request payment under 11 U.S.C. Section 524 (the discharge injunction).

Georgia Federal Bankruptcy Data

Your fresh start begins when the discharge order enters. These Georgia numbers show how reliably Georgia debtors actually reach that order.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,240 consumer bankruptcy cases from Georgia's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 796998.6%0.8%

Chapter 1327171.2%28.8%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Georgia Discharge Pattern

Georgia Chapter 7 cases reach discharge at a strong 98.6% rate. Debtors who file complete schedules and attend their 341 meeting overwhelmingly receive a fresh start here.

Georgia Chapter 13 discharges in 71.2% of resolved cases, above the national average. Plans are more likely to succeed here.

Post-Bankruptcy Credit Rebuild in Georgia

Credit rebuilding after a Georgia bankruptcy typically runs on this timeline:

Month 0-6: Secured credit card approved. Start with a $300-500 secured card, use it for $50-100/month, pay in full. Your FICO starts climbing.

Month 6-12: Second secured card OR a credit-builder loan. The two-tradeline rule pushes FICO above 620 for most filers.

Month 12-18: Auto loan available at subprime rates (12-18% APR). Shop carefully; avoid yo-yo financing.

Month 18-24: Unsecured cards become available. FICO typically 640-680 at this point.

Month 24-36: FHA mortgage eligibility (2-year post-BK wait for Chapter 7; 1 year for Chapter 13 in payment status).

Month 36-48: Conventional mortgage eligibility (4-year wait for Chapter 7).

Year 7: Chapter 13 falls off credit reports (FCRA 7-year rule from filing date).

Year 10: Chapter 7 falls off credit reports.

See detailed credit rebuilding guide.

Georgia Legal Aid and Re-Entry Support

Legal aid resources: Atlanta Legal Aid Society; Georgia Legal Services Program.

Housing consideration: No state-specific BK-tenant protection.

Post-bankruptcy legal aid in Georgia typically covers: follow-up on discharge injunction violations, correction of credit reports, handling reaffirmation agreements, and defending against post-discharge collection attempts.

Buying a Home in Georgia After Bankruptcy

Mortgage waiting periods after Georgia bankruptcy:

Loan TypeChapter 7 WaitChapter 13 Wait

FHA2 years from discharge1 year in payment (with court approval)

VA2 years from discharge1 year in payment (with court approval)

USDA3 years from discharge1 year in payment (with court approval)

Conventional (Fannie Mae)4 years from discharge2 years from discharge / 4 years from dismissal

Conventional (Freddie Mac)4 years from dischargeSame as Fannie Mae

Non-QM / PortfolioAs little as 12 monthsAs little as 12 months

Georgia-specific factor: No state-specific BK-tenant protection.

See full post-BK homebuying guide.

Georgia Employment After Bankruptcy

Federal law (11 U.S.C. Section 525) prohibits most employment discrimination based on bankruptcy:

Government employers (federal, state, local) are expressly barred from discriminating based solely on the bankruptcy filing.

Private employers cannot terminate an existing employee solely because of bankruptcy - but may consider BK in hiring decisions.

Security clearances and licenses generally continue post-BK; some require disclosure but rarely revocation.

Georgia does not add specific private-employer protections beyond Section 525. See post-BK employment guide.

Rebuilding Your Georgia Tax and Financial Profile

A Georgia fresh start also means cleaning up the tax and financial records:

Tax refunds going forward - post-petition refunds are yours; pre-petition refunds may be subject to the trustee's claim depending on timing.

1099-C exposure - bankruptcy-discharged debt is NOT 1099-C taxable income (Sec. 108(a)(1)(A)). This is a major advantage over settlement.

Schedule 1 reporting - federal forms include fields for bankruptcy-discharged amounts; use IRS Form 982.

Retirement contribution resumption - 401(k), IRA, and pension contributions were protected during bankruptcy; now increase them. Retirement is the foundation of permanent financial stability.

First-Year Mistakes to Avoid in Georgia

Common Georgia post-BK mistakes that undercut the fresh start:

Taking on high-interest debt too fast. Predatory subprime lenders target recent filers; payday and title loans are common traps.

Missing the reaffirmation window. Reaffirmation agreements on cars must be filed before discharge; missing this can forfeit the vehicle.

Ignoring post-discharge creditor contact. Collectors who attempt to collect discharged debt violate the Section 524 injunction; keep records and report.

Not reviewing credit reports. Discharged debts should show as "Discharged in Bankruptcy" with $0 balance; incorrect reporting is an FCRA violation.

Co-signing new debt. A co-signed loan that defaults puts your fresh start at risk immediately.

See common post-BK myths and first-year after BK.

Related Georgia Resources

## Life After Bankruptcy in Hawaii [2026]: Credit, Housing, and Fresh Start
Source: https://bankruptcyfreshstart.org/states/hawaii.html

← bankruptcyfreshstart.org home

Life After Bankruptcy in Hawaii [2026]: Credit, Housing, and Fresh Start

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Hawaii residents.

Your Fresh Start in Hawaii

The "fresh start" concept is the core purpose of consumer bankruptcy. Local Loan Co. v. Hunt, 292 U.S. 234 (1934), frames it as giving the honest but unfortunate debtor "a new opportunity in life and a clear field for future effort." In Hawaii, the fresh start has three practical dimensions: debt extinguishment, asset retention, and credit rebuild.

The discharge order under 11 U.S.C. Section 727 (Chapter 7) or Section 1328 (Chapter 13) wipes most unsecured debts permanently. Creditors with discharged debts cannot pursue collection, sue, garnish, or even request payment under 11 U.S.C. Section 524 (the discharge injunction).

Hawaii Discharge Pattern

Federal data for Hawaii is limited; the national baseline applies: roughly 75% of Chapter 7 cases and 45% of Chapter 13 cases reach discharge.

Post-Bankruptcy Credit Rebuild in Hawaii

Credit rebuilding after a Hawaii bankruptcy typically runs on this timeline:

Month 0-6: Secured credit card approved. Start with a $300-500 secured card, use it for $50-100/month, pay in full. Your FICO starts climbing.

Month 6-12: Second secured card OR a credit-builder loan. The two-tradeline rule pushes FICO above 620 for most filers.

Month 12-18: Auto loan available at subprime rates (12-18% APR). Shop carefully; avoid yo-yo financing.

Month 18-24: Unsecured cards become available. FICO typically 640-680 at this point.

Month 24-36: FHA mortgage eligibility (2-year post-BK wait for Chapter 7; 1 year for Chapter 13 in payment status).

Month 36-48: Conventional mortgage eligibility (4-year wait for Chapter 7).

Year 7: Chapter 13 falls off credit reports (FCRA 7-year rule from filing date).

Year 10: Chapter 7 falls off credit reports.

See detailed credit rebuilding guide.

Hawaii Legal Aid and Re-Entry Support

Legal aid resources: Legal Aid Society of Hawaii.

Housing consideration: High COL; post-BK housing search often challenging.

Post-bankruptcy legal aid in Hawaii typically covers: follow-up on discharge injunction violations, correction of credit reports, handling reaffirmation agreements, and defending against post-discharge collection attempts.

Buying a Home in Hawaii After Bankruptcy

Mortgage waiting periods after Hawaii bankruptcy:

Loan TypeChapter 7 WaitChapter 13 Wait

FHA2 years from discharge1 year in payment (with court approval)

VA2 years from discharge1 year in payment (with court approval)

USDA3 years from discharge1 year in payment (with court approval)

Conventional (Fannie Mae)4 years from discharge2 years from discharge / 4 years from dismissal

Conventional (Freddie Mac)4 years from dischargeSame as Fannie Mae

Non-QM / PortfolioAs little as 12 monthsAs little as 12 months

Hawaii-specific factor: High COL; post-BK housing search often challenging.

See full post-BK homebuying guide.

Hawaii Employment After Bankruptcy

Federal law (11 U.S.C. Section 525) prohibits most employment discrimination based on bankruptcy:

Government employers (federal, state, local) are expressly barred from discriminating based solely on the bankruptcy filing.

Private employers cannot terminate an existing employee solely because of bankruptcy - but may consider BK in hiring decisions.

Security clearances and licenses generally continue post-BK; some require disclosure but rarely revocation.

Hawaii does not add specific private-employer protections beyond Section 525. See post-BK employment guide.

Rebuilding Your Hawaii Tax and Financial Profile

A Hawaii fresh start also means cleaning up the tax and financial records:

Tax refunds going forward - post-petition refunds are yours; pre-petition refunds may be subject to the trustee's claim depending on timing.

1099-C exposure - bankruptcy-discharged debt is NOT 1099-C taxable income (Sec. 108(a)(1)(A)). This is a major advantage over settlement.

Schedule 1 reporting - federal forms include fields for bankruptcy-discharged amounts; use IRS Form 982.

Retirement contribution resumption - 401(k), IRA, and pension contributions were protected during bankruptcy; now increase them. Retirement is the foundation of permanent financial stability.

First-Year Mistakes to Avoid in Hawaii

Common Hawaii post-BK mistakes that undercut the fresh start:

Taking on high-interest debt too fast. Predatory subprime lenders target recent filers; payday and title loans are common traps.

Missing the reaffirmation window. Reaffirmation agreements on cars must be filed before discharge; missing this can forfeit the vehicle.

Ignoring post-discharge creditor contact. Collectors who attempt to collect discharged debt violate the Section 524 injunction; keep records and report.

Not reviewing credit reports. Discharged debts should show as "Discharged in Bankruptcy" with $0 balance; incorrect reporting is an FCRA violation.

Co-signing new debt. A co-signed loan that defaults puts your fresh start at risk immediately.

Illinois Discharge Pattern

Illinois Chapter 7 cases reach discharge at a strong 99.5% rate. Debtors who file complete schedules and attend their 341 meeting overwhelmingly receive a fresh start here.

Illinois Chapter 13 discharge rate of 45.9% is typical. Realistic budget assumptions are the main factor in plan survival.

Year 7: Chapter 13 falls off credit reports (FCRA 7-year rule from filing date).

Year 10: Chapter 7 falls off credit reports.

Taking on high-interest debt too fast. Predatory subprime lenders target recent filers; payday and title loans are common traps.

Ignoring post-discharge creditor contact. Collectors who attempt to collect discharged debt violate the Section 524 injunction; keep records and report.

## Life After Bankruptcy in Iowa [2026]: Credit, Housing, and Fresh Start
Source: https://bankruptcyfreshstart.org/states/iowa.html

← bankruptcyfreshstart.org home

Life After Bankruptcy in Iowa [2026]: Credit, Housing, and Fresh Start

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Iowa residents.

Your Fresh Start in Iowa

The "fresh start" concept is the core purpose of consumer bankruptcy. Local Loan Co. v. Hunt, 292 U.S. 234 (1934), frames it as giving the honest but unfortunate debtor "a new opportunity in life and a clear field for future effort." In Iowa, the fresh start has three practical dimensions: debt extinguishment, asset retention, and credit rebuild.

The discharge order under 11 U.S.C. Section 727 (Chapter 7) or Section 1328 (Chapter 13) wipes most unsecured debts permanently. Creditors with discharged debts cannot pursue collection, sue, garnish, or even request payment under 11 U.S.C. Section 524 (the discharge injunction).

Iowa Discharge Pattern

Federal data for Iowa is limited; the national baseline applies: roughly 75% of Chapter 7 cases and 45% of Chapter 13 cases reach discharge.

Post-Bankruptcy Credit Rebuild in Iowa

Credit rebuilding after a Iowa bankruptcy typically runs on this timeline:

Month 0-6: Secured credit card approved. Start with a $300-500 secured card, use it for $50-100/month, pay in full. Your FICO starts climbing.

Month 6-12: Second secured card OR a credit-builder loan. The two-tradeline rule pushes FICO above 620 for most filers.

Month 12-18: Auto loan available at subprime rates (12-18% APR). Shop carefully; avoid yo-yo financing.

Month 18-24: Unsecured cards become available. FICO typically 640-680 at this point.

Month 24-36: FHA mortgage eligibility (2-year post-BK wait for Chapter 7; 1 year for Chapter 13 in payment status).

Month 36-48: Conventional mortgage eligibility (4-year wait for Chapter 7).

Year 7: Chapter 13 falls off credit reports (FCRA 7-year rule from filing date).

Year 10: Chapter 7 falls off credit reports.

See detailed credit rebuilding guide.

Iowa Legal Aid and Re-Entry Support

Legal aid resources: Iowa Legal Aid.

Housing consideration: Small-town tenancy often informal; post-BK reentry typically smooth.

Post-bankruptcy legal aid in Iowa typically covers: follow-up on discharge injunction violations, correction of credit reports, handling reaffirmation agreements, and defending against post-discharge collection attempts.

Buying a Home in Iowa After Bankruptcy

Mortgage waiting periods after Iowa bankruptcy:

Loan TypeChapter 7 WaitChapter 13 Wait

FHA2 years from discharge1 year in payment (with court approval)

VA2 years from discharge1 year in payment (with court approval)

USDA3 years from discharge1 year in payment (with court approval)

Conventional (Fannie Mae)4 years from discharge2 years from discharge / 4 years from dismissal

Conventional (Freddie Mac)4 years from dischargeSame as Fannie Mae

Non-QM / PortfolioAs little as 12 monthsAs little as 12 months

Iowa-specific factor: Small-town tenancy often informal; post-BK reentry typically smooth.

See full post-BK homebuying guide.

Iowa Employment After Bankruptcy

Federal law (11 U.S.C. Section 525) prohibits most employment discrimination based on bankruptcy:

Government employers (federal, state, local) are expressly barred from discriminating based solely on the bankruptcy filing.

Private employers cannot terminate an existing employee solely because of bankruptcy - but may consider BK in hiring decisions.

Security clearances and licenses generally continue post-BK; some require disclosure but rarely revocation.

Iowa does not add specific private-employer protections beyond Section 525. See post-BK employment guide.

Rebuilding Your Iowa Tax and Financial Profile

A Iowa fresh start also means cleaning up the tax and financial records:

Tax refunds going forward - post-petition refunds are yours; pre-petition refunds may be subject to the trustee's claim depending on timing.

1099-C exposure - bankruptcy-discharged debt is NOT 1099-C taxable income (Sec. 108(a)(1)(A)). This is a major advantage over settlement.

Schedule 1 reporting - federal forms include fields for bankruptcy-discharged amounts; use IRS Form 982.

Retirement contribution resumption - 401(k), IRA, and pension contributions were protected during bankruptcy; now increase them. Retirement is the foundation of permanent financial stability.

First-Year Mistakes to Avoid in Iowa

Common Iowa post-BK mistakes that undercut the fresh start:

Taking on high-interest debt too fast. Predatory subprime lenders target recent filers; payday and title loans are common traps.

Missing the reaffirmation window. Reaffirmation agreements on cars must be filed before discharge; missing this can forfeit the vehicle.

Ignoring post-discharge creditor contact. Collectors who attempt to collect discharged debt violate the Section 524 injunction; keep records and report.

Not reviewing credit reports. Discharged debts should show as "Discharged in Bankruptcy" with $0 balance; incorrect reporting is an FCRA violation.

Co-signing new debt. A co-signed loan that defaults puts your fresh start at risk immediately.

See common post-BK myths and first-year after BK.

Your post-BK rights

Iowa means test

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 718,67399.4%0.5%

Chapter 1322,17673.1%26.9%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

Kansas Discharge Pattern

Kansas Chapter 7 cases reach discharge at a strong 99.4% rate. Debtors who file complete schedules and attend their 341 meeting overwhelmingly receive a fresh start here.

Kansas Chapter 13 discharges in 73.1% of resolved cases, above the national average. Plans are more likely to succeed here.

Month 36-48: Conventional mortgage eligibility (4-year wait for Chapter 7).

Year 10: Chapter 7 falls off credit reports.
